description: Use this when a self-employed user or single-member LLC owner asks whether an S-Corp election would save them money. Shows a side-by-side of self-employment tax vs salary-plus-distribution, payroll and compliance costs, California franchise taxes, and the break-even zone.

currently_has_llc.description: Whether the business already operates as an LLC today. Defaults to true. A plain sole proprietorship (no LLC) does not owe the California $800 franchise tax.

expected_net_profit_usd.description: Expected annual net profit (revenue minus business expenses), before any owner salary.

filing_status.description: Filing status for the Additional Medicare Tax threshold. Defaults to single.

licensed_profession.description: Set to physician (or other_ca_licensed for another California licensed profession under Corp. Code 13401) when the work is a licensed professional service. In California such a practice cannot use an LLC, so the comparison becomes sole proprietor vs professional corporation with an S election. Defaults to none.

owner_salary_estimate_usd.description: A reasonable W-2 salary you would pay yourself as an S-corp owner. If omitted, the midpoint of the reasonable-compensation starting range for an owner-services business (about half of profit) illustrates the mechanic. That default is an illustration only - there is no IRS safe harbor at any percentage; use estimate_reasonable_comp for a starting range.

spouse_wages_usd.description: Spouse W-2 wages, used only with mfj (the Additional Medicare threshold is household-level for joint filers).

state.description: US state, 2-letter or name. Defaults to CA. Only California franchise taxes are modeled (the SMLLC gross-receipts fee is excluded; see caveats).

w2_wages_usd.description: W-2 wages from other employers this year (for example a hospital job). They use up the Social Security wage base and the Additional Medicare threshold, which decides whether an S-corp salary saves or costs payroll tax.
